title: Sample Unit (teacher preview)
subtitle: A Tour of the Cabin
martuIntro:
Hi. It is me, Mar'tu. This is not a real lesson, yes? It is a tour of the cabin.
Every kind of page in this course lives here: a lesson, a quiz, a project, two challenges, an article, a cheat sheet and a Quick Check.
Try them all. Nothing here counts toward anything.
Lucky asked what is in it for him. Existing, Lucky. Existing.
goals: Show words on the screen with `print()`
Ask the traveler a question with `input()`

items.title: First Words by the Fire
items.summary: Print words, ask a question, and write a barrier report.

exercises.title: Read the chalk
exercises.martu:
Before we cast anything, we read, yes?
`print()` shows words on the screen. The words go inside quotes. Python calls quoted words a [[string]].
Numbers do not need quotes. A comma lets you print a string and a number on one line.
This code already works. Press Run and read the [[output]].
starter: # Mar'tu's first spell: words in quotes.

checkpoints.text: Press Run and read what prints.
hints: Press the Run button. Pressing Ctrl and Enter together works too.
You do not need to change anything. Just press Run and look at the console.

checks.name: prints the barrier line
checks.code: assert 'The barrier is holding.' in _lines(), 'Press Run to see the barrier line.'

checkpoints.passLine: Oogrish: Steady, now. You read it well.

solution: # Mar'tu's first spell: words in quotes.
exercises.takeaway: `print()` shows words and numbers on the screen.

predict.q: Before you press Run: what will this line print?
predict.explain: The quotes are not printed. The comma becomes one space between the words and the number.

exercises.title: Ask the traveler
exercises.martu:
Someone knocks on the cabin door. I must ask who it is, yes?
`input()` asks a question and waits for an answer. Put the answer in a [[variable]] with `=`.
Then you can [[concatenate|glue]] it to other words with `+`.
In this exercise the traveler always answers `Lucky`. Of course it is Lucky.
starter: # Greet the traveler on the next line.

hints: The traveler's answer is stored in `name`.
Glue words and `name` together with `+` inside `print()`.

checks.name: still asks for a name
checks.code: assert _inputs_used() == 1, 'Keep the input() line so the cabin can ask who is there.'

checks.name: greets the traveler
checks.code: assert any('Lucky' in line and 'Who goes there?' not in line for line in _lines()), 'Print a greeting that includes the name.'

checks.name: uses the variable
checks.code: assert 'Lucky' not in _source, 'Use the variable name instead of typing Lucky.'

exercises.takeaway: `input()` asks a question. `=` keeps the answer in a variable.

exercises.title: The barrier report
exercises.martu:
Every night, someone reports who holds the barrier and how much mana they have left.
A [[variable]] keeps a value under a name. Text needs quotes. Numbers do not.
You cannot glue a number straight onto a string. Turn it into text first with `str()`.
Three small steps, yes? Then the report.

anotherWay.label: Think of jars
anotherWay.text:
A variable is a jar with a label. `caster` is the label. `"Gearshift"` is what is inside.
`str()` is like writing the number on a scrap of paper, so it can join the other words.

1. Type `caster = "Gearshift"` and press Run.
2. Type `mana = 20` on the next line and press Run.
3. Build the sentence: `caster`, then `" has "`, then `str(mana)`, then `" mana."`, joined with `+`.

checkpoints.text: Make a variable called `caster` that holds the text `"Gearshift"`.
hints: A variable is a name, an equals sign, then a value.

checks.name: caster holds Gearshift
checks.code: assert caster == 'Gearshift', 'Store the text Gearshift in caster, with quotes.'

checkpoints.text: Make a variable called `mana` that holds the number `20`.

checks.name: mana is the number 20
checks.code: assert mana == 20, 'Store the number 20 in mana, with no quotes.'

checkpoints.text: Print `Gearshift has 20 mana.` Build it from `caster` and `mana`.
hints: `mana` is a number. Turn it into text with `str(mana)` before you glue it.

checks.name: prints the report
checks.code: assert 'Gearshift has 20 mana.' in _lines(), 'Print exactly: Gearshift has 20 mana.'

checks.name: uses the variables
checks.code: assert _source.count('Gearshift') == 1, 'Use caster in the print line instead of typing Gearshift again.'

bonus.title: What's in it for me?
bonus.text: Lucky wants a report too. Add a line that prints `Lucky has 26 mana.` Use two new variables.
hints: Copy your three lines and change the names and values.

checks.name: prints Lucky's report
checks.code: assert 'Lucky has 26 mana.' in _lines(), 'Print exactly: Lucky has 26 mana.'

checks.name: keeps Gearshift's report
checks.code: assert 'Gearshift has 20 mana.' in _lines(), 'Keep the Gearshift line too.'

campaignLink.why: In the campaign you keep Mar'tu's line in a [[variable]] and hand it to `print_prompt()`. Same idea as `caster`, yes?

exercises.takeaway: Keep values in variables. Use `str()` to glue a number to text.
exercises.pairTalk: Tell your partner why `mana` needs `str()` but `caster` does not. Then each of you types your own report.

items.title: Chalk Quiz
items.summary: Six quick questions, one of each kind.

questions.q: Which line stores the number `20` in `mana`?

whyWrong.0: The quotes make it text, not a number.
whyWrong.2: The name goes on the left of `=`.
whyWrong.3: `==` compares two values. It does not store anything.

questions.explain: The name goes on the left, then `=`, then the value. Numbers have no quotes.

questions.q: What kind of value does `caster` hold?
questions.explain: Quotes make a string. `caster` holds the text `Gearshift`.
`str(hours)` turns `37` into text, and `+` glues the pieces together.

questions.q: Fill the blank so this prints `Shield up.` with a space in the middle.
questions.explain: `+` does not add spaces for you. A space is a string too: `" "`.

questions.q: Put the lines in order so the warning reads from top to bottom.
questions.expectedOutput:
The clock turns red.
Everyone inside the barrier!
Shield up.
questions.explain: Python runs lines from top to bottom, so the output comes out in the same order.

questions.q: Bomb Shell's line crashes. Fix it.
questions.explain: A string needs a quote at the start and at the end. The closing quote was missing.

items.title: The Night Watch Sign
items.summary: Paint a sign for the cabin door.
items.intro:
The night watch needs a sign on the cabin door, yes?
It shows a border, a title, and how many hours are left before the next burst.
items.martu:
I already stored the hours in a [[variable]] called `hours_left`. Do not change it. Use it.
Each task is one line of [[output]]. Press Run after each one.
starter: # hours_left is already set for you. Use it, do not change it.

checkpoints.text: Print a border of exactly ten `=` signs.
hints: A border is just a string of `=` signs.

checks.name: prints the border
checks.code: assert '==========' in _lines(), 'Print a line of exactly ten = signs.'

checkpoints.text: Print `NIGHT WATCH` on the next line.

checks.name: prints the title
checks.code: assert 'NIGHT WATCH' in _lines(), 'Print NIGHT WATCH in capital letters.'

hints: `hours_left` is a number, so it needs `str()` before you glue it.

checks.name: prints the hours
checks.code: assert 'Next burst in 37 hours' in _lines(), 'Print exactly: Next burst in 37 hours'

checks.name: uses hours_left
checks.code: assert '37' not in _source, 'Use hours_left instead of typing 37.'

checkpoints.passLine: Oogrish: A fine sign. Steady hands.

items.takeaway: A project is a few small steps. Run after each one.

items.title: Mar'tu Asks
items.summary: Build Mar'tu's question from the traveler's answer.
items.martu:
Harder now, yes? Ask the traveler to name a place. Build my question from their answer.
The traveler will answer `greenroom`.
starter: # Ask for a place, build the question, then show it.

checkpoints.text: Show `What do you remember about the greenroom?` with `print_prompt()`, built from the answer.
hints: Glue it: `"What do you remember about the " + place + "?"`.
Store that in a variable, then pass it to `print_prompt()`.

checks.name: asks once
checks.code: assert _inputs_used() == 1, 'Ask for the place with input() one time.'

checks.name: shows the question
checks.code: assert 'What do you remember about the greenroom?' in _prompts, 'Show the full question with print_prompt().'

checks.name: builds it from the answer
checks.code: assert 'greenroom' not in _source, 'Use the answer from input() instead of typing greenroom.'

solution: question = "What do you remember about the " + place + "?"

items.title: Asking the Traveler
items.body:
On this site, `input()` does not wait for you to type. Each exercise brings its own answers, yes?
This line asks for a name:
```python
name = input("Your name? ")
```
If the answer is `Gearshift`, the console shows the question and the answer together on one line: `Your name? Gearshift`
Three things to remember:
1. `input()` always hands back a [[string]], even when the answer looks like a number.
2. Keep the answer in a [[variable]], or it is gone.
3. If your code asks more questions than the exercise has answers, Python stops with an `EOFError`.
Run the examples below. Then try it yourself.
